questions.question: Arranged from the lowest frequency to the highest, the electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves to gamma rays, with visible light a narrow band somewhere between them. Which band comes next after radio waves?
choices: Microwaves
Infrared
Ultraviolet
X-rays
questions.context: From the lowest frequency to the highest, the order is radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light from red to violet, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, so the waves grow shorter at every step. Infrared comes one step later, just past the red end of visible light, and ultraviolet and X-rays lie beyond the violet end.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8A; curriculum line G8.P7) teaches the electromagnetic spectrum in order from low to high frequency, radio waves to gamma rays.

questions.question: The colour of light is set by the length of its waves, measured in nanometres, or billionths of a metre. Violet light's waves are about 400 nanometres long. A laser gives off light whose waves are all about 650 nanometres long. What colour is the laser's light?
choices: Red
Blue
Green
Yellow
questions.context: Visible light runs from violet, with the shortest waves at about 400 nanometres, to red, with the longest at about 700, so light of 650 nanometres is red. Blue light's waves are about 450 to 485 nanometres long, green's about 500 to 565 and yellow's about 565 to 590. Red light also has the lowest frequency of all the colours, and violet the highest.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8A; curriculum line G8.P7) teaches visible light as a band from red to violet, its colour set by its wavelength and frequency.

questions.question: William Herschel spread sunlight into its colours with a glass prism in 1800 and moved a thermometer with a blackened bulb from colour to colour. Its readings climbed from violet to red. Then he set the bulb in the dark just beyond the red, and it read warmer than in any colour. What was warming the thermometer there?
questions.answer: Rays in sunlight that eyes cannot see
choices: Rays in sunlight that eyes cannot see
The room, growing warmer as he worked
The glass prism, warmed by the Sun
Its black paint, which warms even in the dark
questions.context: Two more thermometers, blackened the same way, lay out of the light the whole time, and every colour read warmer than they did, so neither the room nor the black paint was warming the bulb. Herschel found that the invisible rays reflect and bend through glass just as light does. They are now known to be a kind of light: he called them calorific rays, and today they are called infrared.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on the electromagnetic spectrum tell how infrared was found, often repeating Herschel's prism-and-thermometer experiment in class (NASA/IPAC activity).

questions.question: Johann Ritter read of William Herschel's invisible heat rays and went looking for more hidden light in 1801. In a dark room he spread sunlight into its colours with a prism, then laid strips of paper soaked in silver chloride, a salt that darkens in light, along the colours and into the dark beyond them. Where did the paper darken fastest?
choices: Just beyond the violet end
Just beyond the red end
In the yellow, the brightest part
In the violet light itself
questions.context: The silver chloride darkened faster in violet light than in red, and fastest of all in the dark just beyond the violet, where no light could be seen: a second invisible band, at the opposite end from Herschel's heat rays. Ritter called them chemical rays; they are now called ultraviolet, which means beyond the violet.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on the electromagnetic spectrum tell how ultraviolet was found, the year after infrared, at the other end of the visible band.

questions.question: Wilhelm Röntgen covered a glass discharge tube in black cardboard at Würzburg in 1895. Each time the tube ran, a coated screen across his darkened room glowed, even with a book of a thousand pages in front of it. When he X-rayed his wife Anna Bertha's hand onto a photographic plate, her bones and wedding ring stood out, and her flesh showed only faintly. Why did her bones show?
questions.answer: Bone stops more of the rays than flesh does
choices: Bone stops more of the rays than flesh does
Bone lets more of the rays through than flesh
Bone gives off rays of its own in the beam
Bone bounces the rays back toward the tube
questions.context: X-rays pass easily through paper, wood and flesh, but dense materials stop more of them, so bone and the metal ring cast shadows on the plate while flesh lets most of the rays through; Röntgen found that lead 1.5 millimetres thick is practically opaque to them. Every X-ray picture of a broken bone works the same way. Bone neither makes rays of its own nor bounces them back: it blocks them.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8B; curriculum line G8.P8) teaches X-rays imaging bones; Röntgen's picture of his wife's hand is the classic first X-ray.

questions.question: Heinrich Hertz made sparks leap across a small gap between two metal rods at Karlsruhe in 1887. Several metres away, a loop of wire with a gap of its own, joined to nothing, gave off a tiny spark each time. Hertz bounced these invisible waves off a zinc sheet, measured how long they were, and worked out how fast they travel. What did he find?
questions.answer: They travel as fast as light
choices: They travel as fast as light
They travel as fast as sound
They travel faster than light
They travel slower than light, faster than sound
questions.context: Hertz's waves, now called radio waves, travel at the speed of light, and he found that they reflect and bend just as light does: they were the waves of electricity and magnetism that James Clerk Maxwell had predicted, of one family with light. Every band of the spectrum crosses empty space at that same speed, while sound, far slower, needs air or another material to carry it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.P7) teaches that every band of the electromagnetic spectrum travels at the speed of light; Hertz's sparks were the first radio waves made and measured.

questions.question: A girl's phone rings in her pocket with a call from a friend in another city. The call reaches her phone from a tower a few kilometres away, with no wire between them. What carries the call from the tower to her phone?
questions.answer: Radio waves, too long for eyes to see
choices: Radio waves, too long for eyes to see
Sound waves, too high-pitched for ears to hear
Sound waves, too faint for ears to hear
An electric current flowing through the air
questions.context: A phone talks to its tower with radio waves, electromagnetic waves like light but far longer than the waves eyes can see, which cross the gap at the speed of light and would cross even empty space. Sound waves are something else entirely, a shaking of air or another material, and the phone's speaker turns the radio signal into sound only at the very end.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8B; curriculum line G8.P8) teaches radio waves at work in wireless technologies such as phones; mistaking them for sound is a known misconception.

questions.question: A microwave oven's magnetron fills its metal box with microwaves about 12 centimetres long. A physics teacher runs one for a minute with two glass beakers inside, one full of water and one empty. The water turns hot, while the empty beaker stays nearly cool. What do the microwaves do to the water?
questions.answer: They twist its molecules to and fro
choices: They twist its molecules to and fro
They break its molecules apart
They fill it with electric charge
They make its atoms radioactive
questions.context: A water molecule has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, so the microwaves' changing electric field twists it back and forth billions of times a second, and all that jostling heats the water. Glass hardly absorbs microwaves, so the empty beaker stays cool, and the oven's metal walls reflect the waves back inside. Microwaves carry far too little energy to break molecules or make anything radioactive, and like every electromagnetic wave they carry no electric charge to leave in the water.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8B; curriculum line G8.P8) teaches microwave ovens as a use of microwaves: the waves make water molecules move and heat up.

questions.question: A rescue helicopter searches a dark forest at night with a thermal camera, and a lost hiker under the trees shows up brightly on its screen. What is the camera picking up from him?
questions.answer: Infrared light given off by his warm body
choices: Infrared light given off by his warm body
Ultraviolet light given off by his warm skin
Faint red light given off by his warm body
Warm air rising from his body to the camera
questions.context: Everything warm gives off infrared light, and a body at about 37 degrees Celsius gives off more of it than the cooler ground and trees, so a thermal camera, which shows small differences in warmth, sees him glow in total darkness, even through smoke. A body only that warm gives off no visible or ultraviolet light, and the camera reads the rays he gives off, not the warm air around him. TV remotes use infrared too, flashing their signals to the set.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on the electromagnetic spectrum teach infrared at work: night and thermal cameras that see warm bodies, and TV remotes.

questions.question: Water treatment plants shine ultraviolet lamps on drinking water to kill the germs in it. A bright red lamp shining on the same water does not kill them. Why can ultraviolet light kill germs where red light cannot?
questions.answer: Each packet of it carries more energy, from its higher frequency
choices: Each packet of it carries more energy, from its higher frequency
Its waves are longer, so they reach deeper into the water
It travels through the water faster, thanks to its higher frequency
Its rays heat the germs, and the heat is what kills them
questions.context: The higher a light's frequency, the more energy each tiny packet of it carries, and a packet of ultraviolet carries enough to damage a germ's DNA so that it cannot multiply, while a packet of red light carries too little, however many arrive. The same energy is why the Sun's ultraviolet burns skin. Ultraviolet's waves are shorter than red light's, not longer, they move through water no faster, and the lamps kill germs by harming their DNA, not by heating them.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8B; curriculum line G8.P8) teaches ultraviolet sterilisation, and that higher-frequency waves carry more energy.

questions.question: Doctors can treat a brain tumour with about 200 thin beams of gamma rays at once, from cobalt sources set all around the patient's head and aimed to cross at the tumour. Why do they not use one strong beam instead?
questions.answer: It would harm all the healthy brain along its path
choices: It would harm all the healthy brain along its path
It would burn only the scalp, as ultraviolet does
It would make the patient's head radioactive
It would bend away from the tumour inside the head
questions.context: Gamma rays pass deep into the body and damage the DNA of the cells along their path, healthy or not. Each thin beam of this machine, the Gamma Knife, is too weak to do much harm on its way, but where some 200 of them cross, the tumour gets a dose that destroys it. Unlike ultraviolet, which is stopped in the skin, gamma rays pass deep through flesh and bone, and rays from a machine outside the body leave no one radioactive.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.8B; curriculum line G8.P8) teaches X-rays and gamma rays in radiation therapy for cancer; their energy harms living cells, so the beams must spare healthy tissue.

Judge (low): the stem's 'where no light could be seen' lent the key its words ('eyes cannot see'); the clause is cut, and 'in the dark' (shared with the black-paint choice) carries the scene. The judge's 'sent out by the tower' was not used, since it would echo the stem's 'tower'. The context now says the waves are far longer than those eyes can see. Stem and wrong choices unchanged.
